# Heterosis, maternal effects and Gardner and Eberhart

\\ \newcommand{\mY}{\mathbf{Y}} \newcommand{\mT}{\mathbf{T}}
\newcommand{\mS}{\mathbf{S}} \newcommand{\mR}{\mathbf{R}}
\newcommand{\vg}{\mathbf{g}} \newcommand{\E}{\mathrm{E}}
\newcommand{\Var}{\mathrm{Var}} \newcommand{\Cov}{\mathrm{Cov}} \\

## 1 Abstract

When the parents are grown beside their crosses, the crosses can be
compared with the parents: the heterosis of each cross, and Gardner and
Eberhart’s split of the crosses into variety effects and heterosis. In a
diallel with reciprocals, the reciprocal effects split into maternal and
non-maternal parts. This vignette takes these three in turn.

## 2 Heterosis

With the parents grown beside the crosses,
[`Heterosis()`](https://myaseen208.com/DiallelAnalysisR/reference/Heterosis.md)
gives for each cross the heterosis over the mid-parent \\MP = (P_i +
P_j)/2\\, the better parent and, if a check variety is named, the
standard variety, in percent, each with a \\t\\ test. With \\B\\
replicates the standard errors of the differences are
\\\sqrt{3MS_E/(2B)}\\ for \\F\_{ij} - MP\\ and \\\sqrt{2MS_E/B}\\ for
the other two.

``` r

het <-
  Heterosis(
      y      = Yield
    , Rep    = Rep
    , Cross1 = Cross1
    , Cross2 = Cross2
    , data   = GriffingData2
    , Check  = 3
    , Better = c("higher", "lower")[1]
    )
het$StdErr
```

       F1_MP    F1_BP
    6.471663 7.472833

head(x = het$Heterosis[order(-het$Heterosis$MP)], n = 6)

plot(x = het, which = c("MP", "BP", "SH", "residuals", "qq")[1])

For traits where a lower value is better (days to flowering, disease
score), `Better = "lower"` takes the lower parent as the better one.

## 3 Maternal and non-maternal reciprocal effects

Cockerham and Weir (1977) write the reciprocal effect of Methods 1 and 3
as \\r\_{ij} = m_i - m_j + n\_{ij}\\: a maternal effect of each parent
and a non-maternal remainder. `Griffing(..., Reciprocal = "split")`
splits the reciprocal line of the analysis of variance accordingly, on
\\P - 1\\ and \\(P - 1)(P - 2)/2\\ degrees of freedom:

``` r

rs <-
  Griffing(
      y          = Yield
    , Rep        = Rep
    , Cross1     = Cross1
    , Cross2     = Cross2
    , data       = GriffingData1
    , Method     = 1
    , Model      = 1
    , Reciprocal = c("combined", "split")[2]
    )
rs$ANOVA
```

                  Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
    gca            7  3804.6  543.52 18.8868 <2e-16 ***
    sca           28 22060.8  787.89 27.3783 <2e-16 ***
    maternal       7    77.7   11.10  0.3856 0.9100
    non-maternal  21   287.9   13.71  0.4763 0.9758
    Error        189  5439.0   28.78
    ---
    Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

``` r

round(x = rs$Maternal, digits = 3)
```

         1      2      3      4      5      6      7      8
     0.087  0.681  0.968  0.830 -0.818  0.196 -1.257 -0.686 

``` r

round(x = rs$StdErr[c("mi", "mi_mj", "nij")], digits = 3)
```

       mi mi_mj   nij
    1.255 1.897 3.285 

Here neither part is significant: the reciprocal differences of this
diallel are small and show no maternal pattern.

## 4 Gardner and Eberhart’s Analyses II and III

For parents and one set of crosses, Gardner and Eberhart (1966) model
the parents by variety effects \\v_j\\ and the crosses by the mean of
their parents plus heterosis. Analysis II splits the heterosis into
average heterosis \\\bar{h}\\, variety heterosis \\h_j\\ and specific
heterosis \\s\_{jj'}\\:

``` r

ge2 <-
  GardnerEberhart(
      y        = Yield
    , Rep      = Rep
    , Cross1   = Cross1
    , Cross2   = Cross2
    , data     = GriffingData2
    , Analysis = 2
    , Model    = 1
    )
ge2$ANOVA
```

                        Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)
    Varieties            7  1850.9  264.41  9.4698 4.546e-09 ***
    Heterosis           28 12529.1  447.47 16.0259 < 2.2e-16 ***
    Average heterosis    1   373.8  373.81 13.3879  0.000398 ***
    Variety heterosis    7  2850.7  407.25 14.5854 3.807e-13 ***
    Specific heterosis  20  9304.6  465.23 16.6619 < 2.2e-16 ***
    Error              105  2931.8   27.92
    ---
    Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

``` r

ge2$Average
```

          Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
    mu_v 84.633437   1.868208 45.301929 9.626013e-71
    hbar  7.750938   2.118349  3.658952 3.980309e-04

``` r

plot(x = ge2, which = c("effects", "specific", "residuals", "qq")[1])
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Analysis III keeps the variety effects for the parents and analyses the
crosses by general and specific combining ability, with average
heterosis between the two; its gca and sca lines are Griffing’s Method
4:

``` r

ge3 <-
  GardnerEberhart(
      y        = Yield
    , Rep      = Rep
    , Cross1   = Cross1
    , Cross2   = Cross2
    , data     = GriffingData2
    , Analysis = 3
    , Model    = 1
    )
ge3$ANOVA
```

                       Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)
    Varieties           7 1574.8  224.96   8.057 8.099e-08 ***
    Average heterosis   1  373.8  373.81  13.388  0.000398 ***
    gca                 7 3126.9  446.70  15.998 3.672e-14 ***
    sca                20 9304.6  465.23  16.662 < 2.2e-16 ***
    Error             105 2931.8   27.92
    ---

## 5 Summary

[`Heterosis()`](https://myaseen208.com/DiallelAnalysisR/reference/Heterosis.md)
compares each cross with its parents and a check;
`Griffing(..., Reciprocal = "split")` asks whether the reciprocal
differences come from the mother;
[`GardnerEberhart()`](https://myaseen208.com/DiallelAnalysisR/reference/GardnerEberhart.md)
describes parents and crosses with one model of variety effects and
heterosis.

## 6 References

of the variety cross diallel and related populations. *Biometrics*,
22(3), 439–452.

Clarification and reevaluation of population-based diallel analyses:

43(6), 1930–1937.
